conclusions: The system lacked a continuous reconciliation loop joining external 287(g) status to active Flock sharing edges.
Control ownership was split:Flock exposed configuration controls, while CPD remained responsible for the changing external eligibility input.
counterarguments: A current 287(g) agreement does not prove an agency used Columbus data for immigration enforcement.
findings: The June 3 cleanup was a point-in-time comparison against then-known 287(g) agencies.
Spartanburg was missed even though its agreement dated to April 2025.
Geauga, Blount, and Cheatham changed eligibility after the cleanup.
Flock said it does not track agencies' changing 287(g) status.
CPD described the resulting monitoring and revocation as ongoing and manual.
limitations: No native configuration export, full roster, or partner-level query log was available.
data.question: Why did agencies prohibited by Columbus policy retain or regain access after the June 3 cleanup?
recommendations: Recover the full edge history and administrator events.
Fail closed when status is unknown or stale.
unresolved: Whether the four agencies queried Columbus before removal.
Who approved and executed each sharing edge.
